alerts.channelEmail: One or more recipients. Requires email to be configured on the deployment.
alerts.channelInApp: A notification in the dashboard. Always available, needs no configuration.
alerts.channelWebhook: Any URL of yours — the alert is posted as JSON. Use this to reach a pager, a ticket system, or your own routing.
alerts.channelsDesc: One channel per rule. Create two rules if you want two.
alerts.conditionsDesc: Four conditions, each evaluated over a window you choose.
alerts.gap1: No PagerDuty or OpsGenie channel. Both accept a plain HTTP endpoint, so the webhook channel reaches them today with a small adapter on your side.
alerts.gap2: No alerting on a schedule or on absence — a rule fires on what happened, not on an endpoint that went quiet when it should not have.
alerts.incidentInvestigating: Somebody has picked it up. The timeline records who and when.
alerts.incidentOpen: Fired and not yet acknowledged by anyone.
alerts.incidentResolved: Closed. The timeline is kept, which is what makes the next occurrence comparable to this one.
alerts.incidentsDesc: Repeated firings of the same rule are grouped into an incident with a timeline, so a week of noise reads as one story rather than forty notifications.
alerts.ssrfDesc: An alert URL goes through the same SSRF protection as a delivery URL: private and loopback ranges are refused unless the deployment explicitly allows them. An alert channel is an outbound request the platform makes on a user's instruction, so it gets the same scrutiny as a webhook.
alerts.ssrfLabel: Webhook and Slack targets are validated
alerts.subtitle: Rules that watch your own traffic and tell somebody when it changes shape.
alerts.title: Alerts and incidents
alerts.tuneMuteDesc: A rule can be muted indefinitely or snoozed until a time. Snooze during a known migration rather than deleting the rule and forgetting to recreate it.
alerts.tuneScopeDesc: A rule can watch one endpoint or the whole project. Per-endpoint is sharper and noisier; project-wide catches a systemic problem that no single endpoint would trip.
alerts.tuneSeverityDesc: Info, warning or critical. It does not change routing — it changes how the alert reads to whoever gets it.
alerts.tuneWindowDesc: How far back the condition looks. Short windows are twitchy on low volume; long windows are slow on high volume. Match it to how many attempts an endpoint actually gets in that time.
alerts.tuningDesc: An alert nobody acts on trains people to ignore the next one. Four settings decide whether that happens.
alerts.twoKindsDesc: Worth separating before anything else, because both appear in a deployment and they watch different things.
alerts.twoKindsLabel: This page is about the first kind
alerts.twoKindsNote: Alert rules are created in the dashboard and watch your endpoints — failure rates, latency, deliveries piling up. Separately, the Helm chart ships Prometheus rules that watch the platform itself: queue depth, breaker trips, the age of the oldest unresolved delivery. Those go to whoever runs Hookflow, not to whoever owns an endpoint. If you self-host, you want both.
alerts.typeConsecutive: A run of failures with no success between them. Catches an endpoint that has gone away entirely, and does it sooner than a rate can — a rate needs volume, a run does not.
alerts.typeDlq: Failed messages accumulating past a count. This is the one that says obligations are being abandoned, not merely retried.
alerts.typeFailureRate: The proportion of attempts that failed, as a percentage over the window. The right choice for an endpoint that is degrading rather than dead.
alerts.typeLatency: Response time above a threshold. An endpoint that answers slowly enough consumes concurrency and will eventually trip the circuit breaker.

auth.apiKeyDesc: A key belongs to one project and travels in the `X-API-Key` header. It is what the SDKs and your servers send events with.
auth.jwtDesc: Login answers with an access token and a refresh token. The access token names the user, their organization and their role, and is what authorizes projects, endpoints, deliveries and everything else the dashboard reads.
auth.refreshDesc: The access token lasts 15 minutes and the refresh token 24 hours, unless the instance was configured otherwise. A refresh returns a new pair and blacklists the refresh token you spent: presenting a spent one again revokes every token that user holds, because a replayed refresh token is what a stolen one looks like. The dashboard refreshes once on a 401 and only surfaces the failure when the refresh token has expired too.
auth.scopesDesc: `READ_ONLY` reads; `READ_WRITE` also writes, which sending an event counts as. A key can carry an expiry date, and a revoked key stops working immediately — there is no grace period.
auth.securityNoteDesc: Only the hash is stored, so a lost key cannot be recovered, only replaced. Keep it in an environment variable on a server you control: a key in client-side code or a repository is a key anyone can send events with.
auth.subtitle: JWT for the dashboard API, API keys for what a project owns.
auth.title: Authentication
auth.usingJwtDesc: Every authenticated request carries the access token in the `Authorization` header:

concepts.attemptDesc: One try at a delivery: one HTTP request and what it resolved to — status, error and latency. The first attempt is not a retry.
concepts.connectionDesc: One endpoint together with the subscriptions that point at it, named as one thing because that is the unit you configure, test and turn off. It is a view, not a record: changing a connection changes the endpoint or its subscriptions.
concepts.deliveryDesc: The obligation to get one event to one endpoint, held until it succeeds or is abandoned. Distinct from the individual tries it takes.
concepts.destinationDesc: A URL you nominated to receive incoming events, together with how to authenticate to it.
concepts.endpointDesc: A URL you registered that is willing to receive events, together with the secret its signatures are computed from.
concepts.eventDesc: Something your system announced happened, with a type and a body. It exists whether or not anything is listening.
concepts.forwardDesc: The obligation to get one incoming event to one destination. The incoming counterpart of a delivery.
concepts.sourceDesc: A third-party provider you have connected, together with what Hookflow needs to prove that a webhook genuinely came from it.
concepts.subscriptionDesc: A standing statement that one endpoint wants events of a given type.

addresses.appBaseUrl: Where your users' browsers reach the dashboard. It is what goes into verification emails, password resets and shared debug links — left on localhost, those links are unusable for everyone but you.
addresses.cors: Origins allowed to call the API from a browser. Comma-separated.
addresses.hookflowBind: Which host interface that port is published on. Installing with a domain moves it to `127.0.0.1` and puts the TLS terminator in front.
addresses.hookflowDomain: The domain the built-in TLS terminator obtains a certificate for. It only runs under the `tls` Compose profile, which `install.sh --domain` turns on.
addresses.hookflowPort: The one port published to the host. nginx serves the dashboard on it and proxies every API path, so it is the single URL to hand out and the single thing to put a certificate on.
addresses.ingressBase: The prefix of the ingress URL shown for each incoming source. It is the URL you paste into Stripe or GitHub, so it has to be the address they can reach, not yours.
addresses.tunnelBase: The same, for the public URL a CLI tunnel prints.
addresses.viteApiUrl: The API origin the dashboard calls. Baked in at image build time, not read at runtime.

configuration.addressesDesc: Every port is a variable — nothing is hard-coded. The two that catch people out are the management port, which is not the API, and the base URLs, which end up inside links your users receive.
configuration.authorityDesc: `.env.dist` is the authority and carries every variable with a comment explaining it — around two hundred, most of them a timeout or a batch size that is right until a load test says otherwise. This page covers the other kind: the ones whose default is a development choice that becomes wrong the moment the instance is reachable from outside your machine.

delivery.allowedHosts: An allowlist of hosts endpoints may point at. Empty means any public host.
delivery.concurrentPerEndpoint: In-flight attempts against a single endpoint. It is a courtesy to the receiver as much as a limit on you.
delivery.fanout: Most deliveries one event may create. An event matching more subscriptions than this is rejected rather than half-delivered.
delivery.gapTimeout: How long an ordered delivery waits for the one before it. After this it goes anyway — a predecessor that never arrives delays one delivery rather than stopping the endpoint.
delivery.payloadSize: Largest event body accepted, in bytes.
delivery.privateIps: Off by default: an endpoint URL resolving to a loopback, link-local or private address is refused, and so are the cloud metadata endpoints. Turn it on only for an instance that delivers exclusively inside your own network.
delivery.projectRate: Events per second one project may send.
delivery.verificationRequired: When on, a new endpoint has to answer a challenge before anything is delivered to it.

configuration.deliveryDesc: The bounds a single project can push the platform to. On a cloud deployment the plan's limits apply on top of these; self-hosted, these are the only ones.

housekeeping.attemptsDays: How long delivery attempts are kept before the nightly cleanup removes them.
housekeeping.billingEnabled: Off means no plans and no quotas — the self-hosted default. On, the seeded plans apply and the limits below stop being consulted.
housekeeping.emailEnabled: Off by default. With it off, verification, invite and reset links are written to the API log instead of sent — which is what makes a local instance usable without a mail server.
housekeeping.entitlementFanout: The fan-out ceiling when billing is off.
housekeeping.entitlementRate: The requests-per-second an organization gets when billing is off.
housekeeping.swagger: Off by default. It publishes the whole API surface, which is a thing to decide about rather than leave on.

configuration.housekeepingDesc: What is kept, what gets sent, and what is exposed.
configuration.howDesc: Everything is an environment variable. `docker compose` reads the `.env` file beside the compose file and passes what each service needs into its container; nothing is configured by editing a file inside an image. Change a value, then `docker compose up -d` — Compose recreates only the containers whose environment changed.
configuration.publicDesc: Four values move together: `APP_BASE_URL` and `VITE_API_URL` for the browser, `WEBHOOK_INGRESS_BASE_URL` and `TUNNEL_INGRESS_BASE_URL` for the providers sending to you. Add the API origin to `CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` and to `VITE_CSP_EXTRA_CONNECT` — the dashboard's Content-Security-Policy blocks any origin it does not name, so a working API and a blank dashboard is what a missed one looks like.

required.adminToken: Presented in `X-Platform-Admin-Token` for the cluster-wide operator endpoints under `/api/v1/admin`, such as rotating the encryption key across every tenant. Deliberately separate from any organization: an org OWNER does not get it. Left empty those endpoints are unreachable, which is the right state until an operator needs them.
required.appEnv: `development`, `staging` or `production`. Production turns on the startup checks below.
required.encKey: Derives the AES-256-GCM key that endpoint secrets, HMAC secrets and mTLS material are encrypted with at rest. Lose it and none of them can be read back.
required.encSalt: The PBKDF2 salt for that derivation. Unique per deployment; changing it has the same effect as changing the key.
required.jwtSecret: Signs every access token. 32 characters or more; rotating it logs everyone out.

configuration.requiredDesc: The shipped values are placeholders. Every one of them is public — they are in `.env.dist` in a public repository — so an instance left on them is an instance anyone can sign tokens for and decrypt the endpoint secrets of.
configuration.startupDesc: With `APP_ENV=production` the services validate their own configuration before accepting traffic and abort on a placeholder secret, a secret shorter than its minimum, or a combination that would leave the instance open. It is a startup failure rather than a warning on purpose: a warning in a log nobody reads is how an instance ends up in production on `dev_jwt_secret_key_32_chars_minimum`.
configuration.startupLabel: What production mode refuses to start on

stores.concurrency: Concurrent consumers per worker instance. Total in-flight deliveries is this times the number of workers, capped by the partition count.
stores.dbMode: `embedded` runs Postgres in Compose; `external` uses the `DB_*` settings below instead.
stores.dbSsl: Set it to `require` for anything not on the same private network.
stores.partitions: Partitions on the delivery topics, which is the ceiling on how many workers can consume in parallel. Raise it before you scale workers past it; it cannot be lowered afterwards.

configuration.storesDesc: Compose runs all three for you. Point them at managed instances when you would rather not operate them: Postgres holds the record, Kafka moves the work, Redis holds the claims, rate limits and the ordering buffer.
configuration.subtitle: The settings a self-hosted instance has to make a decision about, and where each one is set.
configuration.title: Configuration

deterministicReplay.diagAlt: Two lanes. In the retry lane, one delivery loops back to itself for its next attempt, keeping its id and sequence number. In the replay lane, an event produces a second delivery with a new id and a new sequence number, while the original delivery is left unchanged.
deterministicReplay.diagCaption: A retry moves a row you already have. A replay writes a row you did not, and gives it a new position in the endpoint’s sequence.
deterministicReplay.diagFoot: the original is never rewritten by a replay
deterministicReplay.dryRunDesc: dryRun=true answers 200 and sends nothing. It returns the target URL, the event type, the payload, the `Idempotency-Key` that would go out, every previous attempt with its status and error, and a plan line: `WILL_SEND` with the attempt number it would use, SKIP when the delivery already succeeded, or `BLOCKED` when the endpoint is disabled.
deterministicReplay.idempotencyKeyHeaderDesc: Every outgoing request carries one so a consumer can recognise something it has already processed. It is <event key>-<endpoint id> when the event was ingested with an idempotency key, and <event id>-<endpoint id> when it was not. The value is stable across attempts and across a retry of the same delivery. A time-range replay creates new deliveries that carry no key of their own, so they fall back to <event id>-<endpoint id>: if the original event had a key, the replayed request's header will not match the original's.
deterministicReplay.idempotencyPoliciesDesc: Per project, in Settings → Schemas & Policies. Whatever the policy, an `Idempotency-Key` that a project has already used returns the original event instead of creating a second one.
deterministicReplay.oneDeliveryDesc: `POST /api/v1/deliveries/{id}/replay` resets that delivery to `PENDING` with its attempt count back to zero and queues it, answering 202. A delivery that already succeeded is refused with 400 rather than sent twice.
deterministicReplay.policyAuto: An event sent without a key gets a random one. That shapes the `Idempotency-Key` header the receiver sees; it does not deduplicate anything, because two identical requests get two different generated keys.
deterministicReplay.policyNone: A key is used when you send one, and nothing is generated when you do not.
deterministicReplay.policyRequired: An event sent without an `Idempotency-Key` header is rejected with 400.
deterministicReplay.replayFromAttemptDesc: fromAttempt=N sets the attempt count to N-1, so the next request is attempt N and any further waits continue from that tier of the ladder instead of the first. N has to be between 1 and the number of attempts already made; anything else is a 400.
deterministicReplay.replayFromAttemptNote: When restarting at the one-minute tier is the wrong thing to do — a target that was down for hours does not need the short tiers again — or when the ladder is nearly spent and you want the remaining attempts, not a fresh set.
deterministicReplay.retryVsReplayDesc: A retry is the next attempt on the same delivery: same id, same sequence number, ladder continued. A replay of a time range creates fresh deliveries from the stored events, with new ids and new sequence numbers, and leaves the originals untouched. The dashboard calls the second one Time Machine.
deterministicReplay.subtitle: Two operations that are easy to confuse: putting one delivery back on the ladder, and building new deliveries from events you already have.
deterministicReplay.timeMachineDesc: `POST /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/replay` takes a window and creates one delivery per stored event and matching subscription. Ordering-enabled endpoints get fresh sequence numbers, so replayed deliveries queue behind live ones rather than colliding with them. POST .../replay/estimate counts first without creating anything, a session reports its progress while it runs and can be cancelled, and a project runs at most two at a time.
deterministicReplay.title: Replay

endpointSecurity.allowedIpsDesc: Despite the name, this does not restrict anything. It is a place to record which addresses your endpoint expects webhooks from, so the information sits next to the endpoint instead of in someone's notes. Nothing reads it to make a decision. If you need your customers to allowlist Hookflow's outbound address, that is solved at the network layer — see the static egress IP guide in the repository.
endpointSecurity.allowedIpsLabel: A note field, not a control
endpointSecurity.encryptionDesc: Endpoint secrets, client certificates and client keys are encrypted in the database, each row recording which key version encrypted it. Keys can be rotated without downtime: new writes use the new version while old rows are re-encrypted in the background.
endpointSecurity.mtlsCaDesc: Optional. Supply it when the endpoint presents a certificate signed by an authority the platform's trust store does not carry — an internal CA, most often. Without it, an internal endpoint's certificate is rejected before a request is made.
endpointSecurity.mtlsCertDesc: PEM. Presented on every delivery to this endpoint. Encrypted at rest.
endpointSecurity.mtlsDesc: For an endpoint that requires Hookflow to prove who it is at the TLS layer, not just at the signature layer. Enable it and supply the pair.
endpointSecurity.mtlsKeyDesc: PEM, matching the certificate. Encrypted at rest and never returned by the API once stored.
endpointSecurity.rotStep1Desc: A new secret is generated and the current one is kept as the previous. Both are now live.
endpointSecurity.rotStep2Desc: Every delivery carries two signatures, one per secret. A receiver verifying with either one succeeds. It compares against both in constant time, so nothing leaks about which matched.
endpointSecurity.rotStep3Desc: The previous secret stops signing. A receiver still using it now fails verification — which is the point at which you find out whether it was updated.
endpointSecurity.rotTimingDesc: The grace period defaults to 24 hours. That is right for a receiver you control and short for one belonging to a customer who has to schedule a deploy. Widening it after a rotation has started does not help anyone who already stopped receiving the old signature.
endpointSecurity.rotTimingLabel: Choose the window before you rotate, not after
endpointSecurity.rotation: Rotating a secret without breaking the receiver
endpointSecurity.rotationDesc: A secret can be replaced while the old one still works, so the receiver updates on its own schedule rather than during a window you impose on it.
endpointSecurity.ssrf: Where a delivery is allowed to go
endpointSecurity.ssrfDesc: Every delivery URL is validated before a request is built.
endpointSecurity.ssrfLabel: Private ranges are refused by default
endpointSecurity.ssrfNote: Loopback, link-local and private address ranges are rejected unless the deployment explicitly allows them — a self-hosted install delivering to services on its own network legitimately needs that, and it is a deployment setting rather than a per-endpoint one, because it is the operator's decision and not a tenant's. The same check guards alert webhooks.
endpointSecurity.subtitle: Everything on an endpoint that is about trust: rotating its secret, proving who you are to it, and proving it is yours.
endpointSecurity.title: Endpoint security
endpointSecurity.verificationDesc: A URL anyone can type is a URL anyone can point at somebody else. Verification is what stops an endpoint being registered against a host its owner did not consent to.
endpointSecurity.verifyChallengeDesc: Hookflow sends a token to the URL and expects it echoed back. Passing proves whoever registered the endpoint can read responses from it.
endpointSecurity.verifySkipDesc: Verification can be skipped with a recorded reason. The reason is kept on the endpoint, so an unverified endpoint is a decision somebody made rather than a step that quietly did not happen.

errors.code2xx: 201 means something was created — an event, a project, a key. 202 means accepted and carried out afterwards: a replay, or a webhook taken in at an ingress URL.
errors.code400: Malformed, or rejected by validation, a schema policy or a fan-out limit. Read message and fieldErrors and fix the request — retrying will not help.
errors.code401: Credentials missing, expired or wrong. Refresh the JWT, or check the `X-API-Key` header.
errors.code403: Authenticated, but the role or the API key scope does not allow it. A `READ_ONLY` key cannot write.
errors.code404: Nothing with that id exists in this organization. Ids are scoped per organization, so a wrong tenant looks the same as a wrong id.
errors.code409: It already exists, or it changed while you were editing it. Re-read it and send again.
errors.code413: The body is over the limit — 256 KB for the API, 512 KB at an ingress URL.
errors.code429: The rate limit is spent. Wait the seconds given in `Retry-After`, then retry.
errors.code5xx: Hookflow failed. The request is safe to retry with backoff — event ingestion is idempotent when you send an `Idempotency-Key`.
errors.errorFormatDesc: Every error answers with the same shape, so one handler covers all of them. fieldErrors appears only on validation failures and maps a field name to what is wrong with it.
errors.headerLimit: How many requests the current window allows.
errors.headerRemaining: How many of them are left.
errors.headerReset: The Unix timestamp at which the window resets and the budget refills.
errors.headerRetryAfter: Sent with a 429: how many seconds to wait before trying again.
errors.httpStatusCodesDesc: What the API answers, and what to do about it.
errors.rateLimitingDesc: Event ingestion is limited per project, and every answer from `POST /api/v1/events` carries the current budget in these headers. The ingress URL is limited per source instead: it answers 429 with `Retry-After`: 1 and carries no budget headers.
errors.sizeLimitsDesc: A request body over 256 KB is refused with 413; at an ingress URL the limit is 512 KB, because what a provider sends is not yours to shrink. One event also has a limit on how many deliveries it may fan out to — past it the event is rejected with 400 rather than delivered to some of the matching endpoints and not others.
errors.subtitle: The error envelope, the status codes, and the limits behind them.
errors.title: Errors & Limits

gettingStarted.nextDesc: The Test Console sends an event and shows every attempt as it happens. Webhook Security covers verifying the signature; Retries covers what happens while your endpoint is down.
gettingStarted.portActuator: Health and Prometheus metrics, inside the network only. It sits on its own port so a broken auth configuration cannot take health checks down with it; nginx proxies the health paths from it and refuses the rest.
gettingStarted.portApi: The API, inside the Docker network only. Reached through the port above; not published, so nothing outside the network can talk to it directly.
gettingStarted.portWeb: Everything: the dashboard, the API, the docs, the ingress endpoints. The only port bound to the host — nginx serves the dashboard and proxies the rest. Change it with
gettingStarted.portsTitle: The port it binds, and the two it does not
gettingStarted.runBaseUrlDesc: Every sample below points at https://your-api.com — replace it with wherever you put the instance. The health and Prometheus endpoints deliberately sit outside the authenticated chain, on their own port, so a broken auth configuration cannot take your health checks down with it.
gettingStarted.runDesc: Everything below runs against an instance you host. One command installs it: the installer checks the machine, generates your secrets and starts the stack, and everything is served on a single port.
gettingStarted.runSecretsDesc: The .env you downloaded ships development secrets. Set JWT_SECRET, WEBHOOK_ENCRYPTION_KEY and WEBHOOK_ENCRYPTION_SALT to your own values: with APP_ENV=production, startup refuses to complete while any of them is still the shipped default.
gettingStarted.step1Desc: Registration creates the user and the organization everything else hangs off. Login answers with an access token and a refresh token.
gettingStarted.step2Desc: Endpoints, sources, API keys and events all belong to one project.
gettingStarted.step3Desc: The key is returned once, at creation — only its hash is stored. Sending events needs the `READ_WRITE` scope.
gettingStarted.step4Desc: The URL that receives the webhooks, plus the secret its signatures are computed from. It is created unverified.
gettingStarted.step5Desc: Points one endpoint at one event type. Patterns are allowed: order.* matches one segment, order.** any number.
gettingStarted.step6Desc: Answers 201 with the event id, and creates one delivery per matching subscription. The delivering happens afterwards, off the request.
gettingStarted.subtitle: From no instance to a delivered event.
gettingStarted.title: Getting Started
gettingStarted.verifyDesc: A delivery to an endpoint that is neither `VERIFIED` nor `SKIPPED` fails terminally, without a single retry. `POST /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/endpoints/{id}/verify` sends the challenge; Webhook Security has the format of it.
gettingStarted.verifyLabel: It receives nothing until it is verified

incomingWebhooks.dedupDesc: Providers resend. When the request carries an id Hookflow recognises — `X-Webhook-Id`, Stripe-Webhook-Id, `X-GitHub-Delivery`, `X-Shopify-Webhook-Id`, `X-Twilio-Webhook-Id`, or Slack's event_id — a second arrival of the same id returns the stored event instead of forwarding it again. A provider that sends none of these is not deduplicated.
incomingWebhooks.destinationsDesc: A source forwards every verified webhook to each of its destinations. Each destination carries its own retry ladder, timeout and authentication, so a slow internal service cannot hold up the rest.
incomingWebhooks.forwardDesc: Each incoming event creates one forward per destination. A forward walks its destination's own retry ladder — five attempts by default against outgoing's seven — and lands in the DLQ when the ladder is exhausted. Retries has both ladders.
incomingWebhooks.ingressUrlDesc: The token in the path is the only thing that names the source, so the URL is a credential. Verification is what stops whoever learns it from injecting events.
incomingWebhooks.modeHmac: HMAC over the raw body, read from the header name and signature prefix you configure.
incomingWebhooks.modeNone: Nothing is checked — whatever reaches the URL is stored and forwarded. Only while you are wiring a provider up.
incomingWebhooks.modeProvider: The provider's own scheme, picked from the provider type. Every provider type but `GENERIC` has one; `GENERIC` is the label for a provider with no preset, and it is `HMAC_GENERIC` that verifies those.
incomingWebhooks.overviewDesc1: A source is one third-party provider. Creating it mints an opaque ingress URL; what arrives there is verified, stored as an incoming event, and forwarded to every destination on the source.
incomingWebhooks.providerTypes: Provider types: `GENERIC`, GITHUB, GITLAB, STRIPE, SHOPIFY, SLACK, TWILIO.
incomingWebhooks.resp202: Accepted and stored. The body carries the request id.
incomingWebhooks.resp401: Verification is configured and the signature did not check out. Nothing is stored.
incomingWebhooks.resp410: The source exists but is disabled.
incomingWebhooks.resp413: The body is larger than 512 KB.
incomingWebhooks.resp429: The source's per-second limit is spent; `Retry-After` is 1. The limiter fails closed, so it also answers this when Redis is unreachable.
incomingWebhooks.subtitle: One URL per provider, checked on arrival and forwarded to services of yours.
incomingWebhooks.title: Incoming Webhooks

ordering.costDesc: Ordering is not free, and the price is worth knowing before turning it on.
ordering.costHeadOfLineDesc: One slow or failing delivery holds up everything behind it for that endpoint until it resolves or the gap times out. A single endpoint retrying through the ladder can sit at the front of its own queue for hours.
ordering.costReplayDesc: A replay builds a new delivery with a new position, so a replayed event arrives after everything already waiting — not back in its original place. This is what stops a replay from re-blocking an endpoint at a position it passed days ago.
ordering.costThroughputDesc: An ordered endpoint is effectively serial. Deliveries that could have gone in parallel now go one at a time, and the endpoint's own response time becomes your ceiling.
ordering.default: Off by default, and outgoing only
ordering.defaultDesc: Ordering is enabled per subscription. With it off — which is the default — deliveries to one endpoint may overtake each other freely, and that freedom is most of the throughput.
ordering.diagramAlt: Positions 41 and 42 delivered, 43 unresolved, 44 waiting behind it.
ordering.diagramCaption: 44 cannot go while 43 is open. The gap is the whole unresolved range, not only the position immediately before.
ordering.diagramParked: parked — claim released, back to the ladder
ordering.gapTimeoutDesc: A delivery that never resolves would otherwise hold up every later delivery to that endpoint forever.
ordering.gapTimeoutLabel: The guarantee yields rather than blocking
ordering.gapTimeoutNote: After a timeout, the waiting delivery is let through and the gap is counted. Order is broken for that endpoint, on purpose, because an endpoint that has stopped receiving anything at all is the worse failure. The webhook_ordering_gap_timeout_total counter is how you find out it happened — rare is expected, frequent means something upstream is not resolving and ordering is not actually being delivered.
ordering.guarantee1: Order is per endpoint, never global. Two endpoints subscribed to the same event receive it independently, and either may be first.
ordering.guarantee2: Delivery is still at-least-once. Ordering does not make it exactly-once — a receiver can still see the same event twice and should still dedupe on the delivery id.
ordering.guarantee3: The guarantee is best-effort under a gap timeout. If you need order that never yields, you need a sequence number in your own payload that the receiver checks.
ordering.guarantees: What is and is not promised
ordering.guaranteesDesc: Precisely, because ordering is the feature people most often assume means more than it does.
ordering.howItWorksDesc: Every delivery to an endpoint is stamped with a position at creation. A delivery whose predecessors have not resolved waits until they do.
ordering.scopeDesc: Hookflow did not originate a provider's webhooks and cannot know what order the provider intended, so it does not pretend to. Every incoming event is forwarded as soon as it can be. If you need incoming order, the provider's own sequence field in the payload is the only honest source.
ordering.scopeLabel: The incoming direction has no ordering at all
ordering.subtitle: Delivering one endpoint's events in the order they happened, what it costs, and the one case where the guarantee is deliberately broken.
ordering.termBufferDesc: Where a delivery waits while the ones ahead of it are unresolved. It is a cursor in Redis with a database fallback, not a place messages are stored — the delivery itself stays in the database the whole time.
ordering.termGapDesc: The stretch of positions between what the endpoint last received and what is waiting, containing at least one delivery that has not resolved. It is checked as a whole range: looking only at the position immediately before let a delivery several ahead sail through whenever its immediate predecessor happened to be terminal already.
ordering.termSequenceDesc: An endpoint-scoped position stamped on a delivery when it is created. It establishes which of two deliveries to the same endpoint came first, independently of when a worker picks either up.
ordering.title: Ordering

overview.diagDirAlt: Two rows sharing one layout. Outgoing: your system announces order.created, Hookflow delivers it to an endpoint and writes the X-Signature header on the way out, and the attempt rail under the row shows seven rungs. Incoming: a provider posts to Hookflow, which reads the provider's own Stripe-Signature header on the way in and forwards to a destination, with five rungs on its rail.
overview.diagDirCaption: The same platform in the middle both times, and the same attempt rail underneath. What changes is which side of Hookflow the proof sits on: it writes the signature on the way out and reads the provider's on the way in.
overview.diagFanAlt: An order.created event at the top, with three arrows fanning out to three deliveries — one per subscribed endpoint. The first is delivered on attempt 1 of 7, the second is retrying on attempt 3 of 7, and the third has used all 7 and sits in Failed Messages.
overview.diagFanCaption: One event, three deliveries, three attempt counts at the same moment. A delivery that runs out of attempts is abandoned to Failed Messages on its own — nothing about it reaches the two that are still going.
overview.diagFanEach: each delivery walks its own ladder
overview.flow1Desc: `POST /api/v1/events` with a type and a payload. The answer is 201 and the event id.
overview.flow2Desc: One delivery per subscription whose event type matches. Rules run first and can add, redirect or drop them.
overview.flow3Desc: A worker signs the body, POSTs it, and records the status, the response and how long it took.
overview.flow4Desc: A `2xx` ends the delivery. An exhausted retry ladder abandons it to Failed Messages.
overview.incomingDesc: A third-party provider sends a webhook to Hookflow, which proves it came from that provider and forwards it to the destinations you nominated. Hookflow is the receiver.
overview.outgoingDesc: Your system announces an event, and Hookflow carries it to the endpoints your users registered. Hookflow is the sender and signs what it sends.
overview.subtitle: How to send events, receive webhooks, and read what happened.
overview.title: Documentation
overview.whatIsDesc1: Hookflow sends your events to the endpoints your customers registered, and takes webhooks in from other services to forward where you choose.
overview.whatIsDesc2: Both directions share one attempt log, one retry ladder and one set of screens.

piiMasking.defaults: What a new project starts with
piiMasking.defaultsDesc: Three built-in rules are seeded on project creation, all partial. They can be changed or turned off.
piiMasking.displayOnlyDesc: Masking is applied when a payload is rendered. The stored payload is unchanged, and the payload delivered to an endpoint is unchanged. Masking limits who sees a value in the dashboard; it does not stop the value being kept, and it is not an answer to a data-erasure request. If a field must never be stored, drop it before sending the event, or drop it in a transformation.
piiMasking.displayOnlyLabel: This is a display control, not storage or delivery
piiMasking.not1: Not encryption. Secrets and certificates are encrypted at rest separately; masking does not touch storage at all.
piiMasking.not2: Not a delivery filter. Your endpoint receives the unmasked payload — the receiver is trusted, the dashboard viewer may not be.
piiMasking.not3: Not an audit control. Masking changes what a screen shows; it does not record who looked. That is the audit log's job.
piiMasking.ruleTypesDesc: Both are per project, and both can be enabled and disabled without deleting them.
piiMasking.styleFull: Replaces the whole value. Use when even the shape is sensitive.
piiMasking.styleHash: Replaces the value with a stable hash. Two occurrences of the same value look the same, so you can tell that two events concern the same person without learning who.
piiMasking.stylePartial: Keeps enough to recognise the value and hides the rest — the last digits of a card, the domain of an address. The default, because a fully hidden field usually makes the record useless for support.
piiMasking.subtitle: Hide personal data in the dashboard without changing what is stored or what is delivered.
piiMasking.title: PII masking
piiMasking.typeBuiltin: A named pattern Hookflow recognises wherever it appears in a payload, at any depth. You choose the style, not the pattern.
piiMasking.typeCustom: A JSONPath you write, pointing at a specific field. Use this for anything domain-specific — an internal customer reference, a document number, a free-text note.
piiMasking.whatItIsDesc: Rules that redact values in a payload when that payload is shown to a person. A rule names a field — by built-in pattern or by JSONPath — and a style to redact it with.
piiMasking.whereDeliveriesDesc: The request body shown on a delivery and on each of its attempts.
piiMasking.whereDesc: Every surface that shows a payload to a person.
piiMasking.whereDiffDesc: Both sides of a comparison between two events.
piiMasking.whereIncomingDesc: The body kept as it arrived from the provider.
piiMasking.whereSharedDesc: The most important one. A shared link is unauthenticated by design — anyone with the URL can open it — so masking is what makes it safe to send to somebody outside your organization.

reference.lede: Every operation the API serves, generated from openapi.yaml — so it says what the running server actually does.
reference.loadError: The API reference could not be loaded. Reload the page — the index ships with the app, so this is usually a stale cached build.
reference.noMatches: No operation matches this search. Try a path fragment such as /events, or a method such as POST.
reference.searchPlaceholder: Path, summary, operation ID or method…
reference.title: API reference

retries.ageCapDesc: A delivery outstanding longer than 96 hours, or a forward longer than 24, is moved to the DLQ whatever its attempt count says. It exists for obligations that stopped moving — never rescheduled, never claimed — rather than for ones that are failing on the ladder, which the ladder itself ends.
retries.diagramAlt: State diagram. `PENDING` is claimed into PROCESSING, which ends in `SUCCESS` on a `2xx`, in `FAILED` on a result not worth retrying, or in DLQ once the retry ladder is exhausted. A retryable failure sends it back to `PENDING`, and a deferral sends it back without spending an attempt. A dashed arrow marks the second way into DLQ: the age cap.
retries.diagramCaption: The transitions a delivery makes on its own. The manual ones — replaying it, retrying it from Failed Messages — are described below.
retries.dlqDesc: The DLQ — Failed Messages on screen — is where a delivery lands once Hookflow has abandoned it: kept for a person to decide about, not deleted. `GET /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/dlq` is the same list the screen shows: the endpoint URL, the event type, how many attempts were made, the last error and when it was given up on.
retries.dlqRetryDesc: Retrying a failed message resets that same delivery — `PENDING`, attempt count back to zero — and walks the whole ladder again from the first tier. It keeps its delivery id, its sequence number and its `Idempotency-Key`, so a consumer that already processed it sees a duplicate it can recognise.
retries.ladderIncomingDesc: 5 attempts, waiting 1m, 5m, 15m and 1h between them: about 1h 20m nominal.
retries.ladderOutgoingDesc: 7 attempts, waiting 1m, 5m, 15m, 1h, 6h and 24h between them: about 31 hours nominal, up to 47 with jitter at the top of its range.
retries.laddersDesc: Each wait is jittered between 50% and 150% of its tier, so a burst of same-tier retries does not stampede. A delivery carries the ladder of its subscription and a forward the ladder of its destination; these are the defaults when neither sets one.
retries.notCountedDesc: Being turned away before the request is made does not consume an attempt or advance the ladder: a tenant or per-target rate limit, a full concurrency slot, an open circuit breaker, or a delivery held back because an earlier sequence number has not landed. The claim is released and the work is rescheduled. Only requests that were actually made count.
retries.replayDesc: A retry is the next attempt on the same delivery. A replay builds new deliveries from events already stored, leaving the originals as they are — see Replay.
retries.retryableDesc: 408, 429 and any `5xx` are retried, as are a connection error, a timeout, and a transformation that failed to apply. Every other `4xx` is terminal on the first attempt: a 400 or a 404 from your endpoint says the request is wrong, and repeating it will not make it right.
retries.statusDlq: The ladder was exhausted, or the delivery outlived the age cap. Shown as Failed Messages.
retries.statusFailed: Given up on without exhausting the ladder, because another attempt cannot help: the endpoint is disabled, deleted or unverified, its URL is refused by the SSRF check, or the endpoint answered a status that is not worth retrying.
retries.statusPending: Created, or waiting for the time its next attempt is due.
retries.statusProcessing: Claimed by a worker for one attempt. A row left here by a worker that died is handed back to `PENDING` by the stuck sweep, so a crash costs time rather than the delivery.
retries.statusSuccess: The endpoint answered `2xx`. Nothing further is sent.
retries.subtitle: When Hookflow tries again, when it stops, and what it does with what it gave up on.
retries.timeoutsDesc: One attempt waits 30 seconds for the response unless the subscription says otherwise, and a value outside 1–60 seconds is clamped into it. A timeout is recorded as a failed attempt and retried like any other failure.
retries.title: Retries and the delivery lifecycle
retries.whyDifferDesc: Deliberately, and not something to reconcile. Outgoing carries your own event to an endpoint you registered, where holding it for a day is a reasonable promise. Incoming relays somebody else's webhook onward, where a shorter, more decisive give-up is the better one.

rulesEngine.actionDrop: Stop the event here. No delivery is created and nothing is sent.
rulesEngine.actionRoute: Deliver the event to a specific endpoint, whether or not a subscription points at it.
rulesEngine.actionTag: Attach a tag to the event so you can filter on it later.
rulesEngine.actionTransform: Reshape the payload with a saved transformation before it is delivered.
rulesEngine.conceptActionDesc: What happens when the rule matches. A rule can carry several, and they run in the order you set.
rulesEngine.conceptConditionDesc: One test on a field of the payload — a path, an operator and a value. Conditions nest in AND, OR and NOT groups.
rulesEngine.conceptPriorityDesc: Which rule is evaluated first. Higher runs earlier, which decides who gets to drop an event.
rulesEngine.conceptRuleDesc: An event type pattern, a condition tree and the actions to run when both match.
rulesEngine.diagAlt: An order.created event flows into the rules stage, where ROUTE, TRANSFORM and TAG change it and let it continue. A matching DROP action ends it there instead. What survives reaches subscription matching, which creates one delivery per match.
rulesEngine.diagCaption: Rules run before the subscription lookup, which is why DROP is cheap and total: at that point no delivery has been created, so there is nothing to cancel and nothing a customer half-received.
rulesEngine.exampleDesc: Any order over 1000 in USD or EUR is sent to the fraud endpoint and tagged, on top of whatever its subscriptions already do.
rulesEngine.importantBody: Rules are evaluated before subscriptions are matched, so a `DROP` stops the event before a single delivery exists — the event is still stored and still answers 201, it simply goes nowhere. A rule with no conditions matches every event of its type, so give it a narrow event type pattern.
rulesEngine.step1Desc: Your system announces an event through the Events API.
rulesEngine.step2Desc: Enabled rules whose event type pattern matches are collected, highest priority first.
rulesEngine.step3Desc: Each rule's condition tree is evaluated against the payload.
rulesEngine.step4Desc: Every action of a matching rule runs in its configured order.

schemaRegistry.compatBackwardDesc: The new schema can read data written by the old one. A new required property is refused; a new optional one is fine, and so is dropping a property.
schemaRegistry.compatForwardDesc: The old schema can read data written by the new one. Dropping a property the old version required is refused, as is lifting a requirement; adding a property is fine.
schemaRegistry.compatFullDesc: Both directions at once, so a required property may be neither added nor taken away.
schemaRegistry.compatNoneDesc: No promise and no check. The default, and what an auto-discovered schema gets.
schemaRegistry.compatibilityModesDesc: Set per version, and enforced: a version that breaks the promise is refused with 400 rather than stored. Omit it and the previous version's mode carries over. Changing a property's type is refused by all three checking modes.
schemaRegistry.lifecycleAlt: Three states in a row: `DRAFT`, then `ACTIVE`, then `DEPRECATED`. Promoting a draft makes it the active version and moves the version it replaces to deprecated.
schemaRegistry.lifecycleCaption: Only one version is enforced at a time, and promoting the next one is what retires the current one.
schemaRegistry.overviewDesc1: Each event type in a project can carry a JSON Schema. Uploading a version diffs it against the one before and records what changed — fields added, fields removed, types changed, and whether the change breaks a consumer that was written against the older version.
schemaRegistry.overviewDesc2: Validation is off until you turn it on for the project. Once on, every event of a type that has an `ACTIVE` version is checked against it at ingestion, before the event is stored.
schemaRegistry.policyBlockDesc: The event is rejected with 400 and never stored, so no delivery is created.
schemaRegistry.policyWarnDesc: The event is accepted and delivered, and the errors come back on the ingest response so the sender can see what drifted.
schemaRegistry.statusActive: The version every event of this type is validated against. Only one is active at a time.
schemaRegistry.statusDeprecated: Kept for history and diffs. Promoting a new version deprecates the one it replaces.
schemaRegistry.statusDraft: Uploaded but not enforced. Diff it against the active version before promoting it.
schemaRegistry.subtitle: A JSON Schema per event type, versioned, diffed on upload, enforced or not by a per-project policy.

security.diagAlt: Hookflow POSTs to your endpoint. The request carries an `X-Signature` header holding t and v1, computed over the timestamp and the raw body. The receiver recomputes the same HMAC, compares it in constant time, and rejects a timestamp more than 300 seconds old.
security.diagCaption: The signature is over the timestamp and the raw body joined by a dot — not over the body. Hashing the body alone produces a digest that never matches and never says why.
security.diagSigned: signed: <t>.<raw body>, keyed with the endpoint secret
security.diagStep1: recompute HMAC-SHA256 over the same string
security.diagStep2: compare with v1 in constant time
security.diagStep3: reject if t is more than 300 s old
security.endpointVerificationDesc: A new endpoint starts `PENDING` and receives nothing: a delivery to an endpoint that is neither `VERIFIED` nor `SKIPPED` fails terminally without being retried. `POST /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/endpoints/{id}/verify` sends the challenge below and waits 10 seconds for the answer.
security.expectedResponseDesc: Echo the challenge back, either as JSON with a challenge field or as the bare token. Anything else leaves the endpoint `FAILED`, and verification can be run again. An owner can also mark an endpoint `SKIPPED` to deliver to it without the check.
security.headerDeliveryId: This delivery — one event to one endpoint. Unchanged across every attempt of it.
security.headerEventId: The event being delivered. The same event id reaches every endpoint subscribed to it.
security.headerIdempotency: <event key>-<endpoint id> when the event was sent with an idempotency key, and <event id>-<endpoint id> when it was not. Stable across attempts, so a consumer can discard what it has already processed.
security.headerSequence: The endpoint-scoped position of this delivery when ordering is on for the subscription, and 0 when it is off.
security.headerSignature: `t=<unix-ms>,v1=<hex>`. The HMAC-SHA256 of `<t>.<raw body>`, keyed with the endpoint secret. Carries a second `v1` while a rotated secret is inside its grace window.
security.headerTimestamp: The same value as t in the signature: when this body was signed, which is per attempt, not per event.
security.pitfallsDesc: Sign the raw bytes, not a re-serialized object: a reordered or reformatted JSON hashes differently. Compare with a constant-time function. Reject an old `t` — Hookflow allows 300 seconds of skew when it verifies a signature, and five minutes is a reasonable window on your side too. And read every `v1` in the header rather than the first or the last, so a rotation does not look like a forged request.
security.rotationAfter: So the two deploys do not have to be simultaneous: rotate, then roll the new secret out whenever it suits you. Once the window closes the old signature stops being sent. If you verify with a library that reads a single `v1`, deploy inside the window or update it first — the official SDKs already accept either.
security.rotationDesc: `POST /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/endpoints/{id}/rotate-secret` returns a new secret and keeps the old one working. For the endpoint's grace period — 24 hours by default — every delivery is signed with both, and the header carries one `v1` per valid secret:
security.sigVerificationDesc: `X-Signature` is `t=<unix-ms>,v1=<hex>`. `v1` is HMAC-SHA256 over the exact string `<t>.<raw body>`, keyed with the endpoint secret. `t` is milliseconds, not seconds. The header may carry more than one `v1` — see rotating a secret below — so treat the delivery as authentic when any of them matches.
security.standardChoosingDesc: Either, and you can change your mind. An endpoint is sent both header sets by default, and a receiver ignores the headers it does not read, so the choice costs nothing to defer and nothing to revisit — verify `X-Signature` today, move to the Standard Webhooks headers when it suits you, and no deploy of yours has to line up with one of ours.
security.standardChoosingWhere: Reach for the Standard Webhooks headers when you would rather add a dependency than write signing code, or when you already verify another provider the same way. Reach for `X-Signature` when you have working verification code for it. Narrow an endpoint to one set only once nothing is reading the other — on the Connections tab, beside that endpoint’s signing secret.
security.standardDesc: Every delivery also carries the Standard Webhooks headers — `webhook-id`, `webhook-timestamp` and `webhook-signature` — unless the endpoint is set to send only `X-Signature`. It is the convention OpenAI, Anthropic, Twilio, PagerDuty and Supabase send, so there is a verification library for it in most languages and you write no signing code of your own.
security.standardHeaderId: The delivery id — one event to one endpoint, unchanged across every attempt of it, and part of what is signed. Safe to deduplicate on.
security.standardHeaderSignature: `v1,<base64>`. HMAC-SHA256 over `<webhook-id>.<webhook-timestamp>.<raw body>`, keyed with the endpoint’s `whsec_…` secret. Space-separated, one entry per valid secret while a rotated secret is inside its grace window — so treat the delivery as authentic when any of them matches.
security.standardHeaderTimestamp: When this body was signed, in unix seconds — not the milliseconds `X-Timestamp` carries on the same request. Do not hand one to a verifier expecting the other.
security.standardPitfallsDesc: Sign the raw bytes, as with `X-Signature`. Then the three that belong to this scheme alone: the timestamp is seconds, so a milliseconds comparison rejects everything; the digest is base64, not hex; and `webhook-id` is part of the signed string, so leaving it out produces a digest that never matches and never says why. Read every space-separated entry in `webhook-signature` rather than the first, or a rotation looks like a forged request.
security.standardSecretDesc: Not the same string. `X-Signature` is keyed with the endpoint secret as it is; the Standard Webhooks headers are keyed with that same secret in the conventional `whsec_<base64>` form. The API returns it as `standardWebhooksSecret` whenever it returns the secret itself — at creation and at rotation — and the dashboard shows it beside the other. The official SDKs accept a raw secret too and use it as-is, so handing over the wrong form fails as an invalid signature rather than as an error that says which one you meant.

transformations.attachDelivery: Whatever was resolved is written onto the delivery when it is created. Editing a template later does not change a delivery already in flight — it keeps the version it was created with.
transformations.attachDestination: The incoming direction's equivalent, on the destination a forwarded webhook goes to.
transformations.attachRule: A rule whose condition matched can apply a transformation as its action, overriding the subscription's.
transformations.attachSubscription: The default for every delivery this subscription creates. The common case.
transformations.attachingDesc: Four places, and they resolve in that order for a given delivery.
transformations.diagramAlt: Claim, then transform, then sign, then send. A failed transformation stops before the signature.
transformations.diagramCaption: The transformation sits between the claim and the signature. Nothing is sent if it fails.
transformations.dryRunDesc: Resolve the template against a real stored event and see the exact body that would be sent, including how the subscription and any matching rules resolved. Still sends nothing.
transformations.limitMetricDesc: The transform_failed_total counter rises whenever a template fails to resolve. A steady rate means a template is broken for a shape of payload you did not anticipate.
transformations.limitMissing: A missing path is empty, not an error
transformations.limitMissingDesc: JSONPath expressions that match nothing resolve to nothing rather than failing the template. This keeps an optional field optional — and it means a typo in a path is silent. Use the preview.
transformations.limitVersionDesc: Each save increments the version. Deliveries record which one they used, so an attempt from last week can be explained by the template that was live last week.
transformations.notJsDesc: There is no JavaScript, no JSONata and no sandbox. A template can read the payload and rearrange it; it cannot loop, call out, or compute. That is a deliberate limit — arbitrary code in the delivery path is a whole class of outage that a template cannot cause.
transformations.previewDesc: Run the template against a payload you paste in and see the result. No delivery is created.
transformations.rawDesc: If the template fails to resolve, the attempt fails and is retried — the original payload is not sent in its place. This is one of the attempt runner's stated invariants. A template fixed within the retry ladder still gets the event out; a template that is never fixed sends nothing at all, which is the safe direction to fail in.
transformations.rawLabel: A broken template never leaks the raw payload
transformations.studioDesc: An editor with the payload on one side and the result on the other, updating as you type.
transformations.subtitle: Reshape a payload before it is signed and sent, without touching the event your application announced.
transformations.templateDesc: A transformation is a JSON template with JSONPath expressions in ${…} placeholders. The placeholders are resolved against the event payload; everything else is copied through literally.
transformations.testing: Testing one before it is live
transformations.testingDesc: Three ways, in increasing order of how much they exercise.
transformations.title: Transformations
transformations.whenItRunsDesc: Inside the attempt, after the claim is held and before the signature is computed. The order matters: the signature covers the transformed bytes, so a receiver verifying the signature is verifying what it actually received.

workflows.dagDesc: The graph is directed and acyclic: a node cannot feed back into one that already ran. The builder refuses to save an edge that would close a loop.
workflows.execFailureDesc: A failed node ends its branch and the run is marked failed. Other branches finish, and every step keeps the error it recorded. Nodes have their own timeout, and the run as a whole has one too.
workflows.execOrderDesc: Nodes run in topological order, so a node never starts before everything it depends on has finished.
workflows.execParallelDesc: A node with several outgoing edges fans out, and each branch carries its own copy of the payload.
workflows.execTracingDesc: Every step stores its input, its output and how long it took, so a run can be read back node by node in the execution history.
workflows.howItWorksDesc: A workflow is a graph of nodes. A trigger starts it, and each node's output becomes the next node's input.
workflows.nodeCreateEvent: Announces a new event back into Hookflow, which its own subscriptions then pick up.
workflows.nodeFilter: Tests the payload and stops the branch when it does not match. Everything downstream is skipped.
workflows.nodeHttp: Calls an external URL and passes the response on. Private and loopback addresses are refused.
workflows.nodeSlack: Posts a message to a Slack webhook URL.
workflows.nodeTransform: Reshapes the JSON payload before it moves on.
workflows.nodeTrigger: Where the workflow starts. It receives the event that set the run going.
workflows.sec1: HTTP and Slack nodes call out to the network. Their URLs go through the same SSRF checks as an endpoint, so private and link-local addresses are refused.
workflows.sec2: A step stores its input and output verbatim. Anything secret in the payload is readable in the execution history — mask it with a PII rule first.
workflows.sec3: A workflow runs with the permissions of the project it belongs to and can reach nothing outside its organization.
workflows.subtitle: A graph of steps that runs when an event arrives: test it, reshape it, call a service, or announce a new event.

faq.a1: 10,000 events a month, 3 projects, 5 endpoints per project, 5 team members and 7 days of payload retention. Retries, signatures, Failed Messages, replay, analytics and the audit log are all included — no credit card, and nothing expires after a trial.
faq.a2: Hookflow retries on a ladder — 1m, 5m, 15m, 1h, 6h, 24h for outgoing, one rung shorter for incoming. When the rungs run out, the delivery moves to Failed Messages with every attempt and response kept, and waits there for a person to retry it or let it go.
faq.a3: Every delivery carries an HMAC-SHA256 signature over the timestamp and the raw body, with a secret unique to that endpoint. The Node, Python and PHP SDKs ship a verification helper; anything else is a few lines with a standard HMAC library.
faq.a4: Outgoing: your system announces an event and Hookflow delivers it to the endpoints your customers registered — Hookflow is the sender and signs. Incoming: a provider posts to a URL Hookflow owns, the signature is verified, and the payload is forwarded to the destinations you nominated — Hookflow is the receiver. Both share one attempt log and one set of screens.
faq.a5: Yes — it is the same code. The self-hosted build is MIT licensed with every feature on and no limits on events, projects, endpoints, members or retention. One command installs it, and pointing it at a domain gets it a TLS certificate of its own.
faq.a6: The dashboard shows usage against your plan as you approach it, and you can change plan at any time from Billing. Rate limits are per second, so a burst is smoothed rather than dropped.
faq.a7: Per endpoint, yes. Each delivery carries a sequence number, and a delivery whose predecessor is still retrying waits its turn instead of overtaking it.
faq.a8: Any of them. Stripe, GitHub, GitLab, Slack, Shopify and Twilio verify with no configuration — each has a verifier written for the exact header it sends. For any other provider that signs its body with a shared secret, name the header and the prefix and Hookflow verifies it the same way. A provider that does not sign at all can still deliver; the payload is stored and forwarded, marked unverified.
